stops.headline: s4-services

statement.text: Firmware builds the services that everything later will call.

screens.support: The firmware's own source names this stage DXE, and this recording holds none of its drivers, only what it left in the TPM log.

evidence.label: Not recorded: the recording holds no list of the drivers that built these services.
evidence.caption: What the recording has for this stop is six records about Secure Boot policy. The first this project places here is record 4, below.

detail.console_note: The firmware printed nothing on the console during this stage.
detail.explanation: UEFI 2.11 does not describe this stage. It describes what a conforming system must provide: a table of services that later software calls, and a record of which device offers which service. This recording has no list of the drivers that built those services, so none is shown. What the recording does have for this stop is six records in the TPM log, all about Secure Boot policy.

definitions.definition: A piece of firmware code that offers a service or runs a device. UEFI says a driver's start-up code may not touch hardware; it only announces what it can do.
The firmware's list of handles, each with the services (protocol interfaces) attached to it.

claims.text: Every conforming system must provide the system table, the boot services and the runtime services.
Once firmware is initialised it passes control to the boot manager. UEFI 2.11 says nothing about how the firmware reached that point.
The handle database is a list of handles, each with one or more protocol interfaces.
How the firmware stores that database is its own choice.
Connecting drivers to devices is a platform job. UEFI says the boot manager usually does it and allows other designs.

That the services come into being at this stage is the common account of the stage named DXE. It is not from UEFI 2.11, and neither the firmware's source nor the Platform Initialization specification was read to confirm it.
The firmware's own module naming uses the letters DXE: the console prefix is BdsDxe.

statement.text: Before any check, firmware records the rules it will check by.
statement.emphasis: the rules it will check by

screens.support: Five records in a row go to TPM register 7: the Secure Boot switch, the owner's key, the update key, the allowed list and the forbidden list.

evidence.caption: The second of the five policy records: the owner's key.

detail.console_note: No console line belongs to these records.
detail.explanation: Secure Boot is the thread that can block, and its policy is five stored variables: a switch, two keys and two lists. UEFI 2.11 defines what each one means and who may change it, but not that they are recorded in the TPM or in which register; that belongs to a Trusted Computing Group document that has not been read for this project. What is shown here is what this firmware did: five records, in this order, all in register 7, before any record about a loaded program. The file recording.json keeps each record's size and digest, and the raw log stored beside it, eventlog.bin, keeps the value itself: for the switch that is one byte, 01.

definitions.definition: The type name the log decoder gives these records. The firmware's public header lists it with the code 0x80000001, the code this recording holds.

claims.text: Five events in a row, at positions 3 to 7, record the variables SecureBoot, PK, KEK, db and dbx, in that order, all in register 7.
claims.field: events[3..7] (index fields 4 to 8): pcr, type, summary

claims.text: In the log these five records come before the first record about a loaded program, which is at position 25.
The SecureBoot variable is set before any image is checked and should not change afterwards in that boot.
A value of 1 in SecureBoot means the firmware checks driver and boot program signatures during this boot. A value of 0 means it does not.
How SecureBoot gets its starting value is left to platform policy, with one limit: it must be 0 in setup mode or audit mode.
The Platform Key links the platform's owner to the firmware, and the Key Exchange Key links an operating system to the firmware.

claims.text: An update to db or dbx is accepted only from a signer that chains to a Key Exchange Key certificate, or from the Platform Key.
db is the authorised signature database and dbx is the forbidden one.

stops.label: Choosing what to boot

stage_name.name: BDS
stage_name.attribution: A name from the firmware's own source and from the Platform Initialization specification, which was not read for this project. UEFI 2.11 calls this part the boot manager; the letters BDS occur in it once and are not defined there.

claims.text: BDS is commonly written out as Boot Device Selection. The document that defines the name was not read for this project.
UEFI 2.11 describes a boot manager: firmware policy, set through stored variables, that loads programs in the order those variables give.
The firmware's boot manager prints its console lines under the prefix BdsDxe.
claims.source: observed in recording normal-1 console line 0

stops.headline: s5-boot-order

statement.text: Now firmware decides what to start.

screens.support: The boot manager, which the firmware's source names BDS, reads a stored list of boot options and must try them in that order.

evidence.caption: The stored order, as the firmware recorded it.

events.note: Four records the decoder labels platform configuration: ACPI DATA.

detail.console_note: The console line for this stop is on the next screen.
detail.explanation: UEFI 2.11 is firm here: for a normal boot the firmware must use the stored boot order, first entry first. It also leaves room: the firmware may add options or remove invalid ones, and a change to the order is only guaranteed to act after a reset. The recording shows the order variable, four bytes that the raw event log beside it holds as 00 00 01 00, and two boot options written to register 1, after four configuration records in the same register. That these go to register 1 is what this firmware did; the rule for it is in a Trusted Computing Group document that has not been read for this project.

claims.text: For a normal boot the firmware must use the boot order held in the stored variables.
BootOrder is an ordered list; its first element is the first option to try.
The firmware may add boot options or remove invalid ones, and a change to the order is only guaranteed to take effect after the next reset.
The recorded BootOrder variable has 4 data bytes.
Four bytes is room for two 16-bit entries. This is a reading of the size against the UEFI format.

The four bytes are 00 00 01 00 in the raw event log stored beside the recording. Read as two 16-bit numbers with the low byte first, they are 0000 and then 0001, the numbers in the names of the two options recorded after it.
claims.field: events[13] (index field 14); the value is in eventlog.bin, beside this file

claims.text: Two boot option variables are recorded after it: Boot0000 with 62 data bytes and Boot0001 with 110.
Four records before them, also in register 1, are labelled platform configuration: ACPI DATA. This project does not know what requires them.
